Canonical `choices:` arrays for escalation decision points. Command bodies are authoritative; where
`/document` and `/epics` differ for the same scenario, both variants are listed.

## §0 — Array shape: two to four options, and the free-text option is the harness's

**Every `choices:` array in this plugin and in every plugin that depends on it carries between two
and four options, and never authors an "Other" option of its own.** `AskUserQuestion` renders
`minItems: 2, maxItems: 4` and supplies the free-text escape itself — its own schema says *"There
should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically."* A five-option array is not a
long prompt; it is a tool call the harness rejects at validation, so the run cannot present it at
all.

This replaces the rule that stood here, which said the opposite: that every array ends in
`"Other… (describe)"` and that adding one where a phase omitted it was a permitted adjustment. That
rule authored 136 duplicate options across 30 files and pushed 42 arrays past the cap, and it did it
while the file next to it insisted the arrays be presented verbatim — a rule the harness made
unfollowable.

**Two consequences, both of which the rest of `escalation-rules` now depends on:**

1. **The free-text option is unconditional.** No array can decline it. A picker that used to protect
   a closed vocabulary by *omitting* the option cannot do that any more, and must handle the answer
   instead — see *Closed-vocabulary pickers must normalise the free-text answer*.
2. **A fifth option must go somewhere else, not away.** Where an offer has more routes than four,
   `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/references/next-phase-offer.md`'s *overflow rule* applies: the prose carries
   every route, the array carries the likeliest, and the run says the list is longer than the prompt
   in the question's own text, after `Not shown as an option:`, naming every option the array leaves
   out; it never says so only in text printed before the question.

**A selection carries no text.** Choosing an option returns its label and nothing else. An option
that needs text from the operator — a name, a path, a key, a reason, a correction — is labelled
`… (you'll be prompted)` or `… (you'll be prompted for <what>)`, whatever the rest of its wording,
and choosing it is followed at once by one plain-text question asking for that text (one exception:
where *Manual fix notes — the run drafts them* has the run draft the notes, the prompt *Provide
manual fix notes (you'll be prompted)* promises is that section's picker of the draft, whose *Write
my own notes* asks the plain-text question); the run never reads the bare selection as a refusal
or as a promise the operator broke. Its label never words the
text as a promise or an instruction the selection itself would have to carry out (`— name it`,
`I'll say which`, `give the reason`, `(enter the path)`). A free-text answer in the harness's own field that already carries
the text is taken as given, and nothing is asked again. A question whose whole answer is text with
no default — a name, a URL, a reason — and no other way on is asked in plain text: never as a picker
built for it, and never with an "I'll provide it" option. **An array whose other option is a real
alternative is not built for the text, and stays** — a *Cancel* that ends the run the way the prose
after the array states, a *Skip*, a way on without the text: its text option carries the marker
above and is followed by the plain-text question, and the prose after the array — or the rule of
this reference it cites, which states it for every citer — says what each other option does. An alternative no prose handles is not a real one: write its handling there.
What this forbids is an array with no real alternative to offer, which is asked as a plain-text
question instead. A plain-text question may still name its own way out in the question itself
(`…, or type cancel`), as the *Branch prefix undetected* identity variant does, and needs no array
for it.

## Choice lists are presented verbatim

**A choice list written into a command phase is presented to the user verbatim. Its options, their
order, their wording, and the `(Recommended)` marker are not the orchestrator's to change. An
orchestrator that believes a different option is correct for this run says so in prose alongside the
list — it never edits the list.**

This rule binds every command in the family — this plugin's own and those of every plugin that depends on it — not only the ones `escalation-rules` documents. It exists because a
`/document` run presented Phase 6.5's `["Run smoke-check (Recommended)", "Skip — use the manual table
only", "Cancel"]` with the recommendation moved onto Skip, and the render gate was never exercised.

There is no permitted adjustment. Under §0 an array's options are exactly what its phase wrote, and
the free-text option is the harness's — neither is the orchestrator's to add to or take from.

## The `(Recommended)` marker is unconditional

**A `(Recommended)` marker applies whenever its list is shown.** A marker that carries its own
condition — `(Recommended for <case>)`, `(Recommended if <case>)` — is malformed: it hands the user
the gate the command was supposed to evaluate, and it cannot be honoured verbatim by an orchestrator
that must not edit the list. Write it one of two ways instead:

- the condition **gates the prompt** (the list is only shown in that case) → the marker is a plain
  `(Recommended)`; or
- the condition **lives in the option's own description** → the list carries no marker at all.

A **reason** annotation is not a condition and is fine: `(Recommended — <why>)` states why the option
is recommended, unconditionally, and is honoured verbatim like any other marker (`/document`
Phase 5 and `/epics` Phase 1 both use it).

**A marker the command resolves through a placeholder is not a violation of this rule, and it is not
an edit to the list.** Where which option is recommended varies per showing, the array may carry a
placeholder the command substitutes — `/brd-split`'s Phase 4 walk writes `<recommended>` on each of
its dispositions and resolves it, per row, to `(Recommended — <why>)` on one and to the empty string
on the rest. That is substitution, exactly as `<BRD-KEY>` and `<merge-clause>` are substituted in
the same strings (`references/next-phase-offer.md`'s *Resolving this placeholder is not a rewording*), and it is the mechanism this section's first
bullet asks for: the **command** evaluates the condition and prints a bare, reasoned marker, rather
than printing the condition for the user to evaluate. What stays forbidden is the orchestrator
deciding a marker belongs somewhere the command did not put a placeholder.

When no option is safe to recommend across the runs that reach a prompt, omit the marker and say so
in prose beside the list (as `/document` Phase 5.6 does for its per-occurrence image review).

This rule binds every command in the family — this plugin's own and those of every plugin that depends on it — not only the ones `escalation-rules` documents.

## When a choice list fires

**A choice list blocks whenever it is shown.** Presenting one and continuing without an answer is never
correct — the list *is* the wait.

**A list is shown only when its firing condition holds.** A list with no written condition is shown
every time its phase runs. That is the default, and it is the right default for most phases.

**A list written for a question whose answer is already determined is a defect**, not a formality — it
spends a user turn on a prompt with one plausible answer. Where the answer is determined on some runs
and open on others, write the firing condition and keep the list for the runs where it is open.

**The inline-confirmation form.** When the answer is determined, state the resolution in one line that
names what was resolved and how to correct it, then proceed without waiting:

```
Reading this as a <type> — say so if it's actually a <other-type>.
```

An inline confirmation is **not** a choice list: it carries no `choices:` array, it never waits, and the
run continues on the stated resolution. It is the correct form wherever a phase would otherwise ask a
question with one plausible answer.

This rule governs only *whether* a list is presented. Option wording, option order, and the
`(Recommended)` marker are governed by *Choice lists are presented verbatim* and
*The `(Recommended)` marker is unconditional*, and are untouched by it.

This rule binds every command in the family — this plugin's own and those of every plugin that depends on it — not only the ones `escalation-rules` documents.

## key dir not found

`choices: ["Re-enter key (you'll be prompted)", "Cancel"]`

Used when the address resolved to no folder — `resolve-address` returned `status: absent`, or a
folder that resolved earlier in the run is gone when a later phase reads it. *Re-enter key* is
followed by one plain-text question for the key, which is read and resolved as the original address
was (`workflows-core:addressing` §1, §3). *Cancel* ends the run there, the stop standing as it
would with no list.
**A folder that is there is never this case, whatever it holds**: re-entering a key that resolved
cannot help. A command that stops on what such a folder holds — a BRD container, a folder placed at
no level, a PRD folder carrying no key, a PRD folder with no `prd.md` — raises a named stop of its
own instead, as `/document`'s and `/release-notes`' `*_BRD_NOT_SLICED`, `*_FOLDER_NOT_PLACED`,
`*_PRD_NO_KEY` and `*_NO_PRD` do. (The
folder read is an inline step each command performs, not an agent returning a status — this rule
described a dispatch that no longer exists.)

## Required path environment variable unset

`choices: ["Set <VAR> (you'll be prompted for the path)", "Cancel"]`

Used when a command stops — or, for `REPOS_PATH`, asks — because a path environment variable it
requires is unset, or resolves to nothing that exists. `<VAR>` is that variable's own name, written out — the list names the variable
the run is missing, never a generic placeholder. *Set <VAR>* is followed at once by one plain-text
question for the path (§0, *A selection carries no text*); the answer — for `REPOS_PATH` one
directory or a colon-separated list — is carried as `$<VAR>` for the rest of the run once it names
an existing directory (for a list, once one of its entries does), and the question is asked again
where it does not. *Cancel* ends the run there, the stop standing as it would with no list, save
where a citer below says otherwise.

`/brd-intake` (Phase 0 step 5), `/prd-ground` (Phase 0 step 3 for `SPECS_PATH` and Phase 0 step 7
for `REPOS_PATH`), `/brd-split` (Phase 0 step 2, and for `REPOS_PATH` Phase 7's *Ground now*
step 2, borrowing `/prd-ground`'s step 7, where *Cancel* drops the continuation rather than
ending the run), `/brd-interview` (Phase 0 step 3), `/brd-package`
(Phase 0 step 3), `/brd-reconcile` (Phase 0 step 3), `/frames` (Phase 0 step 0), `/prd-proposal`
(Phase 0 step 1), `/brd-proposal` (Phase 0 step 1), `/idea` (Phase 0 step 1),
`/security-workflows:scan` (Phase 0 step 3, on every run), `/implement` (Phase 0
*Address resolution*, on a `<KEY>` address only), `/document` (*Mode detection*, keyed mode on a
`<KEY>` address only, and for `REPOS_PATH` keyed mode's Phase 1), `/release-notes` (Phase 0
step 1, on a `<KEY>` address only, and for `REPOS_PATH` Phase 1, with diff grounding on),
`/conformance` (Phase 0 step 2), `/ready` (Phase 0 step 2), `/create-prd` (Phase 0 step 2b),
`/update-prd` (Phase 0 step 2), and — for `SPECS_PATH` and `REPOS_PATH` both — `/design` (Phase 0
step 2, and Phase 1 step 4), `/specify` (Phase 0 step 2, and Phase 1 step 4), `/create-ard` (Phase 0
step 2, and Phase 1 step 3) and `/epics` (Phase 0 step 0a, and Phase 1, with code examination on)
cite this rule by name. **`REPOS_PATH` is
asked for only where no entry of `${REPOS_PATH:-/workspace}` is an existing directory**: a value
that resolves is used without a question, and `/design`, `/specify`, `/create-ard`, `/epics`,
`/document` and `/release-notes` print it on a `Repos:` line instead. **Where a citer's run can go on
without code, its array carries that run's own way on between the two options** — `/specify` *Proceed without code scan*, `/create-ard` *Ground only the
confirmed-mounted set (record the rest as open questions)*, `/epics` *Turn code scan off — produce
Epic drafts from PRD content alone*, `/document` *Proceed without the repos — PRD-only for every
repo*, `/release-notes` *PRD content only* — and no option is marked; `/design`, `/prd-ground` and
`/brd-split`'s *Ground now* cannot run without code, and keep the two-option list. A citer this rule
does not name for `REPOS_PATH` requires `SPECS_PATH` alone (`/idea --ground-code` reads
`${REPOS_PATH:-/workspace}` with its default and never stops on it; a `$DOCS_PATH` that does not
resolve only skips documentation grounding, or, in `/document`, one rung of its docs-repository
ladder, and stops nothing). **State the set by its
property, not by counting from the end of the list, nor by naming a subset**: the clause read "for
the last four" until the list grew, at which point it silently described a different set, and a
named subset that replaced it then left `/brd-split` and `/brd-intake` out of it. Derive the set
rather than trusting this list:
`grep -rl 'Required path environment variable unset' plugins/*/commands/*.md`, run from the
repository root. For `SPECS_PATH` it is a stop, not a degradation: there is no "continue without
it" option, because that path is where the run's inputs and outputs live. `REPOS_PATH` holds only
code a run reads, which is why a citer whose run can go on without it offers that way on. No
command offers *Set <VAR>* without naming this rule in the same paragraph — `scripts/check-docs.sh`
check 23 holds that, so a command never carries a typed path on its own terms; a citer uses the list
written here, save the `REPOS_PATH` way on, which this rule gives a citer whose run can go on
without code.
